newsitem.title: USA: Union reports progress on jet issue with American.
newsitem.headline: Union reports progress on jet issue with American.

text.p: The pilots union on Saturday reported progress in resolving a dispute with American Airlines over commuter flights, but said it had not yet decided whether to back American's new contract proposal.

James Sovich, president of the Allied Pilots Association, added that after two days of union discussions on the contract proposal, the APA would not make any more concessions to avert a threatened strike by its pilots set for April 28.

He said the issue of who is to fly the new small jets American is to buy for its regional carrier, American Eagle, remained the most contentious in its agreement in principle with American, the nation's No. 2 airline.

Sovich said that negotiators for the APA pilots, who fly American's big jets, have an understanding with the Air Line Pilots Association, who fly Eagle's turboprops, on who would fly the commuter jets, but American had not yet signed on.
There was no immediate comment from American, a unit of AMR Corp..
Last Wednesday APA and American reached its agreement in principle, but the APA's board must endorse the pact and then send it to its 9,300 members for ratification.

Sovich told reporters he did not know when the board might vote, adding its constitution says it must have the proposal in contract language for seven days before it can vote, but officials said this could be waived.
Officials said the board, with a waiver, could vote later on Saturday or postpone action into next week.

Sovich said the agreement in principle included the issues of overall pay, cost of living increases and pay scales for new big American jets, but that who is to fly the new small regional jets was still "the most contentious issue."
He said a "hybrid" solution was reached with Eagle's pilots union, the Air Line Pilots Association, but it was not yet in writing so could not be considered by the board.

Sovich gave no details of the hybrid agreement, saying only it would allow lower-paid Eagle pilots move to the big jets when American was hiring and for American's higher-paid pilots to move to Eagle planes if American was contracting.
One union official said if Eagle pilots were allowed to fly regional jets, "We're concerned American will expand the regional fleet and shrink the American fleet."

Even if the board accepts American's proposal, membership approval would not be assured. After the board accepted an American proposal last Sept. 2, the members rejected it on Jan. 8, setting the stage for the new dispute.

The union went on strike at midnight on Feb. 14 following a week of fruitless negotiations, but minutes later the White House created the Presidential Emergency Board, sending the pilots back to work.
Under PEB law, the pilots are prohibited from striking for 60 days while the board tries to fashion a proposed settlement and the two sides consider whether to accept it.
They agreed to extend the deadline to April 28.

From the beginning cockpit rights to the new jets was a contentious issue, with American wanting its Eagle pilots, who make an average of $35,000 a year, to fly them, rather than APA pilots, who make $120,000 a year.
American has said that it needed the lower-paid pilots in order to be competitive with low-cost commuter carriers flown by its rivals.
But the APA argued that the commuter jets have a range of 2,000 miles (3,200 km) and American can easily put them on routes now flown by its big jets flown by APA pilots, costing APA jobs.
The PEB tried to bridge the difference by recommending that American limit the number of commuter jets flown, the routes they fly and the airports they serve.
